title: The Embarrassing Initiation
text:
In the late 1950s at Stanford, Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills recruited female students to join a discussion group about the psychology of sex. Before joining, each woman was told she had to pass a screening test.

For some, the test was severe: they had to read aloud, to the male experimenter, a list of obscene words and explicit passages from novels. For others, the test was mild, with a few sexual but not embarrassing words. A third group joined with no test at all.

Each woman then listened through headphones to what she believed was an ongoing discussion by the group she had joined. In fact it was a recording, designed to be as dull as possible: a halting, boring conversation about the sexual behavior of animals, full of hesitations and contradictions.

Asked to rate the discussion and the group members, the women who had gone through the severe initiation rated both as much more interesting and likable than the women in the mild or no-test conditions did. The authors explained this through cognitive dissonance: having suffered to get in, people justify the effort by valuing what they gained.
lesson: People value what they suffered to join, even if it is dull. Be wary of loyalty that comes from hazing, and judge a group by what it actually offers.
source: Aronson, E., and Mills, J. (1959). The effect of severity of initiation on liking for a group. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 59(2), 177-181.
